summary: For ages 9–11, build the full causal chain behind Sun-driven weather: uneven solar heating → temperature differences → air-pressure differences → wind (air flowing high-to-low) → ocean currents → large-scale weather patterns. Anchor with the concrete land-sea breeze (land heats and cools faster than water) then scale the same mechanism to the Equator-pole gradient. Introduce air pressure explicitly as the new linking idea beyond a simpler 'what causes wind' topic. A manipulable model where the learner varies the Sun's input and watches circulation respond is proposed to make the heating→pressure→wind chain felt rather than asserted; a hands-on sand-vs-water investigation and a rotating-globe view support and extend it.
misconceptions: Wind has no cause / just 'happens' — it is air flowing because heating created a pressure difference
Land and water heat at the same rate — land heats and cools much faster than water
Air pressure is unrelated to wind — pressure differences are precisely what drive wind
The Sun heats the whole Earth evenly — uneven heating (angle, surface) is the whole driver
Ocean currents and winds are separate from the Sun rather than both driven by its heating

activities.title: Run the 'Sun engine' planet
steps: Use a Sun-input control to heat the Equator more than the poles (or land more than sea at local scale) and observe pressure cells build and colour in response.
Watch air visibly stream from high-pressure regions to low-pressure regions as wind, and ocean currents loop away to carry the heat.

Turn the Sun's input DOWN (which in this model also shrinks the heating difference between places) and observe the whole system — winds, currents, weather bands — slow to a crawl; then turn it back up.
Toggle the same model between a local land-sea breeze cross-section and the global Equator-pole scale to see it is one engine at every size.
Say aloud the chain for one case: uneven heating → warmer air rises/expands → pressure difference → cooler denser air flows in = wind.
activities.insight: One driver — uneven solar heating — powers the whole planetary weather machine through the pressure differences it creates; the same basic mechanism operates from a coastal breeze up to global circulation, though at the global scale Earth's spin also bends the winds and currents.

activities.title: Sand vs water under a lamp (fair-test investigation)
steps: Place equal-depth trays of dry sand and water, both starting at room temperature, side by side under a desk lamp at the same distance.
PREDICT, with reasons, which will warm up faster while the lamp is on, and once the lamp is off, which will cool down faster.
Measure both with thermometers placed at the same shallow depth, at regular time intervals while heating and while cooling, and compare results to the prediction.
State what the temperature difference means for air above each surface and how that could start a breeze.
activities.insight: Land (sand) heats faster and cools faster than water under the same Sun input; this differential heating is what sets up the temperature — and then pressure — differences that drive a sea breeze.

activities.title: Trace the chain and reverse the night-time case
steps: Given the daytime land-sea breeze, order the steps: uneven heating → warm air rises/expands → lower pressure over land → cooler higher-pressure air over sea flows in → wind.
Explain what changes at night when the land cools below the sea temperature, and predict the reversed wind direction with a reason.

Transfer the chain to the global scale: explain how the Equator receiving more direct sunlight than the poles sets up pressure differences that drive large-scale winds (which Earth's spin bends into planet-circling belts) and ocean currents that loop.
activities.insight: The same uneven-heating-to-pressure-to-wind chain explains both the day and reversed night breeze and scales up to global atmospheric and oceanic circulation.

activities.title: Globe view of whole-planet circulation
steps: Rotate a globe showing a warm Equator and cold poles with large-scale flow bands.
Point out where warm air rises and where circulation returns, relating the bands to the flat cross-section model.
Describe how the circulation wraps the sphere rather than lying in one flat plane.
activities.insight: Global circulation genuinely wraps a rotating sphere, so a 3D view adds authentic spatial insight into how Equator-to-pole cells and currents span the planet.

activities.title: Narrate the engine with an expert (optional stretch)
steps: Ask a climatologist (or role-play one) to narrate how the Sun runs the planet's weather, step by step.
Check the narration includes the pressure step and connects winds, currents and weather to a single driver.
Compare the verbal account to what you saw in the model or investigation.
activities.insight: The chain can be told as a coherent story linking one driver to many systems, reinforcing the mechanism in words.

checkQuestion: On a sunny day, dry land warms up much faster than the sea beside it. How does that difference in heating end up making wind blow — what's the chain from 'the Sun heats things unevenly' to 'the air moves'?
checkAnswer: The Sun heats land and sea unevenly; air over the warmer land heats, expands and rises, leaving lower pressure there; denser, higher-pressure air over the cooler sea flows in to fill the gap — that flow is wind. Scaled up (equator vs poles), the same uneven heating drives global winds, ocean currents and weather systems.
